PHSCS 587

Transport over and through barriers

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how carriers access a contact by thermionic emission or tunneling

A contact barrier filters carrier energies. Thermionic emission uses carriers with sufficient thermal energy to pass over its top. In a simple ideal Schottky model, the thermionic current scale has a strong factor exp[−qφB/(kBT)], with barrier voltage φB and temperature T. The prefactor depends on the band structure and emission model.

Field emission tunnels through a sufficiently thin barrier from energies close to the occupied carrier supply. Thermionic-field emission combines thermal access to elevated energies with tunneling through the remaining barrier. The three arrows separate energy routes; they do not represent classical motion through a forbidden region. Doping, electric field and temperature help select the dominant route.

A depletion width can shrink with increasing doping or bias, making tunneling important even when a barrier height remains. Conversely, a wide barrier can suppress tunneling so that thermal activation dominates. Interpreting a measured I–V curve therefore benefits from temperature dependence, doping information and a consistent barrier profile, rather than fitting every contact to one exponential law.

Example

For thermionic-dominated transport at fixed barrier and a suitable prefactor model, raising temperature increases the fraction of carriers able to reach the barrier top. A tunneling-dominated contact can show a much weaker thermal activation.

Practice

1. What distinguishes thermionic-field emission from pure thermionic emission?

Identify the last part of the route.

Carriers first gain thermal energy but still tunnel through a remaining forbidden region; pure thermionic carriers pass over the barrier top.
